Cioè: vorrei che mastro Ford: That is to say: I would wish that Master Ford

Cioè: vorrei che mastro Ford.meaning: I would wish / I would like (1st sing. conditional)

Cioè: vorrei che mastro Ford: Falstaff clarifies his brazen fantasy: he wishes Alice's husband Master Ford were dead so that he could make her his titled wife.
might pass to a better life...

passasse a miglior vita....meaning: might pass / should pass (3rd sing. imperfect subjunctive)

'Passare a miglior vita' is a classic Italian euphemism for dying ('to pass to a better life'). The imperfect subjunctive 'passasse' is governed by 'vorrei che'.
Perché?: Alice feigns innocent incomprehension with a blunt, one-word question, leading Falstaff further into his boastful trap.
Perché? Lo chiedi?: Falstaff feigns incredulity that Alice should even ask why he wishes her husband were out of the way. Clitic 'lo' represents the proposition.
Saresti la mia lady: Falstaff tempts the bourgeois Alice with social elevation: as the wife of a knight, she would bear the aristocratic title of 'lady'.
e Falstaff il tuo lord!: Falstaff pairs 'lady' and 'lord' in English aristocratic terminology, grandly presenting himself as her noble partner.

Povera lady inver!.meaning: in truth / indeed (apocopic form of invero)

Povera lady inver!: Alice counters with mock-modest irony: 'inver' (apocope of 'invero') punctures Falstaff's pomposity.
Falstaff escalates his extravagant courtly flattery, elevating Alice from a lord's lady to someone fit for royalty itself.
T'immagino fregiata del mio stemma,: I imagine you adorned with my coat of arms,

T'immagino fregiata del mio stemma,.meaning: coat of arms / crest / heraldic emblem

T'immagino fregiata del mio stemma,: Falstaff imagines Alice decorated with his knightly crest ('stemma'), continuing his aristocratic seduction rhetoric.
mostrar fra gemma e gemma: Apocopic infinitive 'mostrar' governed by 't'immagino': Falstaff envisions Alice displaying her bosom framed by radiant gemstones.
'Sen' is poetic apocope for 'seno'. Falstaff blends sensual admiration with courtly grandeur ('pompa').
Nell'iri ardente e mobile dei rai: In the fiery and shimmering rainbow of rays

Nell'iri ardente e mobile dei rai.meaning: in the iris / rainbow (in + l' + iri, poetic for iride)

Nell'iri ardente e mobile dei rai: Elevated poetic diction by Boito: 'iri' (rainbow/prismatic refraction, classical for iride) and 'rai' (poetic plural of raggio), describing diamond brilliance.
dell'adamante,: 'Adamante' is classical poetic Italian for diamond (from Greek adamas), elevating Falstaff's courtly imagery to epic heights.
col picciol piè nel nobile: with the tiny foot in the noble
Poetic apocopes 'picciol' and 'piè'. Falstaff evokes Renaissance lyric tropes of feminine delicacy.
cerchio d'un guardinfante: A 'guardinfante' (farthingale) was an Elizabethan hooped petticoat worn by aristocratic ladies to support wide skirts.

risplenderai!.meaning: you shall shine / glitter (2nd sing. future)

risplenderai!: The 2nd person future 'risplenderai' resolves Falstaff's sweeping period ('Nell'iri ardente... col picciol piè... risplenderai!').
More dazzling than an ample rainbow.
'Arcobalen' uses poetic apocope for meter and rhyme with 'sen'. Falstaff rounds off his extravagant compliment comparing Alice to a shimmering rainbow.
Ogni più bel gioiel mi nuoce e spregio: Every finest jewel harms me and I despise
Alice counters Falstaff's aristocratic fantasies with a show of virtuous bourgeois modesty, asserting that opulent jewelry only encumbers her.
Alice scorns golden luxury as a 'finto idolo' (false idol), highlighting her deliberate contrast to Falstaff's superficial material values.
Mi basta un vel legato in croce, un freg: A veil tied in a cross suffices me, an ornament

Mi basta un vel legato in croce, un freg.meaning: criss-crossed / crosswise / in the form of a cross

Mi basta un vel legato in croce, un freg: Alice describes her simple, modest middle-class attire: a humble veil crossed over her chest ('legato in croce') instead of jewels.
at the waist and on my head a flower.
Alice completes her picture of rustic charm: a ribbon at her waist ('cinto') and a single flower in her hair ('un fior').
Sirena!: Falstaff cries out 'Sirena!', captivated by Alice's enchanting singing and her seductive display of simple innocence.
Adulator!: Alice delivers a teasing rebuff with poetic apocope: 'Adulator!' (flatterer), keeping Falstaff in playful suspense.
Soli noi siamo: Inverted word order ('Soli noi siamo') gives dramatic weight to their supposed privacy as Falstaff presses closer.
Falstaff reassures Alice that they are safe from surprise—a classic moment of dramatic irony since Meg and Quickly are waiting outside.
Io t'amo!: Falstaff makes an emphatic declaration of love with explicit subject pronoun 'Io', stepping forward boldly.
Voi siete nel peccato!: Alice checks Falstaff's advance with feigned pious reproach, reminding him of the sinfulness of seducing a married woman.

Sempre l'amor l'occasïone azzecca..meaning: hits upon / seizes / strikes right (3rd sing. present)

Boito writes 'occasïone' with a diaeresis for four poetic syllables (oc-ca-si-o-ne). 'Azzeccare' colloquially means to hit the mark or seize an opportune moment.
Sir John!: Alice feigns moral shock, using his full title 'Sir John' to remind him of chivalric decorum.
Whoever follows their calling does not sin.
Boito borrows directly from Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1: ''Tis no sin for a man to labour in his vocation.' Falstaff humorously rationalizes his lust as a divine calling.
I love you! and it is not my fault...
Falstaff pleads irresistible romantic compulsion: loving her is beyond his control, hence he is entirely blameless.
If you have such vulnerable flesh.
Alice delivers a hilarious double-edged retort: Falstaff's flesh ('polpa') is vulnerable not just spiritually, but because there is an enormous amount of it!
Quand'ero paggio: Opening of Falstaff's famous 30-second miniature arietta ('Quand'ero paggio'), one of the most celebrated moments of vocal agility and charm in late Verdi.
del duca di Norfolk ero sottile,: to the Duke of Norfolk I was slender,
Direct Shakespearean allusion to Henry IV Part 2, where Shallow recalls young Jack Falstaff serving as boy page to Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk.
ero un miraggio: Falstaff poetically characterizes his youthful, slender form as an ethereal apparition or mirage ('miraggio').
Verdi sets the rapid adjectives with feather-light staccato sixteenth notes; the repetition 'gentile, gentile' conveys nostalgic delight.
Quello era il tempo del mio verde aprile: That was the time of my green April,
'Verde aprile' is a classic Renaissance poetic trope symbolizing the fresh springtime of life and youthful vigor.
quello era il tempo del mio lieto maggio: that was the time of my joyful May.
Falstaff pairs 'verde aprile' with 'lieto maggio'. The lowercase initial in the libretto reflects the syntactic parallel with the previous line.
Tant'ero smilzo, flessibile e snello: I was so slim, supple and slender
Falstaff piles up three synonymous terms for lithe svelteness ('smilzo, flessibile e snello'), creating an irresistible comic contrast with his massive bulk.
that I would have darted through a ring.
Boito adapts Falstaff's boast from Henry IV Part 1: 'I could have crept into any alderman's thumb-ring.' 'Guizzare' evokes slipping through like an agile fish.

Voi mi celiate..meaning: you jest / you tease / you mock (2nd plural present)

'Celiare' means to banter or jest. Alice plays along coyly, pretending to suspect Falstaff is making fun of her.
Alice feigns apprehension that Sir John is a predatory seducer whose flattering words are calculated traps.
The present subjunctive 'amiate' is triggered by 'temo che'. Alice sets the trap, pausing suggestively before naming Meg.
Chi?: Falstaff is startled by the unexpected suspicion of infidelity, blurting out a quick interrogative.
Alice springs her trap, naming Meg Page—the very woman to whom Falstaff sent a carbon-copy love letter.
Her? Her face is repulsive to me.

Colei? M'è in uggia la sua faccia..meaning: she / that woman (distal demonstrative, often dismissive)

'Essere in uggia a qualcuno' is a vivid idiom meaning to be intensely disagreeable or loathsome. Falstaff ruthlessly denounces Meg to flatter Alice.
Alice drops his formal knightly title and calls him intimately 'John...', disarming his caution and inflaming his desire.
Mi par mill'anni: It seems a thousand years to me

Mi par mill'anni.meaning: a thousand years (idiom for intense longing/impatience)

Mi par mill'anni: 'Parere mill'anni a qualcuno' is an Italian idiom meaning to wait with unbearable longing ('I cannot wait another second').
to have you in my arms.

d'averti fra le braccia..meaning: to have you (di + avere + clitic ti)

'Braccia' is the irregular feminine plural of 'il braccio'. Falstaff lunges forward to sweep Alice into his embrace.
Falstaff breathes out his ardent declaration as he moves to hold Alice, right before the scheduled interruption.

Per carità....meaning: for heaven's sake / for pity's sake

Idiomatic plea 'Per carità' ('For heaven's sake / Have mercy'). Alice dodges his grasp exactly as the planned disruption begins.
Vieni!: Imperative of 'venire': Falstaff demands her compliance just as Quickly's voice rings out.
Signora Alice!: Quickly shouts from offstage according to the women's plot, abruptly shattering the romantic rendezvous.
Chi va là?: Falstaff responds with an instinctive military sentinel challenge ('Chi va là?'), startled by the sudden voice.
Mia signora!: Quickly rushes into the room displaying feigned breathless panic, playing her part in the staged intrusion.
C'è mistress Meg, e vuol parlarvi, sbuff: Mistress Meg is here, and she wants to speak to you, she puffs...

C'è mistress Meg, e vuol parlarvi, sbuff.meaning: to speak to you (parlare + clitic vi)
she huffs / puffs / snorts (3rd sing. present)

C'è mistress Meg, e vuol parlarvi, sbuff: Quickly creates an alarming theatrical scene, describing Meg as snorting with rage ('sbuffa') outside the door.

strepita, s'abbaruffa....meaning: she clamors / rants / makes an uproar (3rd sing. present)
she brawls / scuffles / wrangles (3rd sing. present reflexive)

Quickly heaps up energetic verbs: 'strepitare' (to roar noisily) and 'abbaruffarsi' (to scuffle/brawl), terrifying Falstaff with Meg's supposed fury.
Alla malora!: 'Alla malora!' is a common Italian oath/curse meaning 'Curse it!' or 'To the devil with it!'.
And she wants to enter and I can barely hold her back...

E vuol passare e la trattengo a stento...meaning: I hold back / restrain (1st sing. present)

'A stento' is an adverbial idiom meaning 'barely' or 'with great difficulty'. Quickly pretends she is barely able to physically restrain Meg.

Dove m'ascondo?.meaning: to hide oneself (poetic variant of nascondersi)

Dove m'ascondo?: 'Ascondersi' is the classical/literary equivalent of 'nascondersi'. Falstaff instantly panics at the thought of being caught by Meg.
Alice points Falstaff to the folding screen ('paravento'), setting the stage for one of the greatest farcical concealment scenes in opera.
Falstaff si rimpiatta dietro il paravent: Falstaff crouches behind the folding screen. When Falstaff is hidden,

Falstaff si rimpiatta dietro il paravent.meaning: crouches / conceals himself (3rd sing. present reflexive)

Falstaff si rimpiatta dietro il paravent: Stage direction: 'Rimpiattarsi' comically depicts Falstaff attempting to compress his massive girth behind the narrow screen.
Quickly fa cenno a Meg che sta dietro l': Quickly signals to Meg who is behind the right door: Meg enters
Stage direction showing the conspiratorial stagecraft of the women: Quickly signals Meg to enter right on cue.
fingendo d'essere agitatissima. Quickly: feigning to be extremely agitated. Quickly exits again.

fingendo d'essere agitatissima. Quickly.meaning: to exit / go out (archaic variant of uscire)

fingendo d'essere agitatissima. Quickly: Stage direction: 'Escire' is the archaic form of 'uscire'. Meg enters feigning hysterical agitation ('agitatissima').
Alice! che spavento!: Meg begins her theatrical performance with loud exclamations of terror for the benefit of the concealed Falstaff.
Che chiasso! Che discordia!: Meg escalates the tension with exclamatory pairings ('chiasso' and 'discordia') describing the imaginary riot outside.
Non perdere un momento,: Negative imperative in the 2nd person singular: 'non' followed by the infinitive 'perdere'.
Urgent imperative of 'fuggire'. Meg orders Alice to run away, increasing the dramatic pressure on Falstaff.
Misericordia!: Alice acts her role in the charade, crying 'Misericordia!' with mock-pious distress.
Che avvenne?: Passato remoto of 'avvenire' ('what occurred? / what happened?'). Alice prompts Meg to deliver the alarming backstory.
Il tuo consorte: 'Consorte' is formal literary Italian for spouse, adding mock-solemnity to Meg's report of Ford's fury.

vien gridando «accorr'uomo!».meaning: help! / to the rescue! (ancient hue and cry)

vien gridando «accorr'uomo!»: 'Accorr'uomo!' (literally 'run, man!') is an ancient Italian hue and cry, summoning neighbors to stop a criminal or fire.
Meg pauses theatrically with an ellipsis, ratcheting up the suspense for the eavesdropping Falstaff.
Alice whispers an aside to Meg telling her to speak louder so Falstaff behind the screen doesn't miss a single word.
MEG Che vuol scannare un uomo!: MEG That he wants to slaughter a man!

MEG Che vuol scannare un uomo!.meaning: to slaughter / butcher / cut the throat

MEG Che vuol scannare un uomo!: The libretto text includes the speaker label 'MEG'. 'Scannare' is a visceral verb meaning to slit someone's throat or butcher like livestock.
Alice whispers a quick aside warning Meg not to betray the trick by bursting into laughter.
Ei correva: Meg resumes her breathless account of Ford's approach. 'Ei' is a literary/poetic truncation of 'egli' (he).
invaso da tremendo: 'Invaso da' denotes being possessed or overcome by an uncontrollable maniacal passion.
furor! Maledicendo: 'Furor' is poetic apocope for 'furore'. The gerund 'maledicendo' captures ongoing, frantic rage.
tutte le figlie d'Eva!: 'Le figlie d'Eva' is a classic poetic/biblical idiom for all womankind, blamed by jealous men for deceit.
Dice che un tuo ganzo hai nascosto,: He says that you have hidden a lover of yours,
'Ganzo' is a colorful, colloquial Italian term for an illicit lover, paramour, or gigolo.
he wants to discover him at any cost...

lo vuole ad ogni costo scoprir....meaning: at all costs / whatever it takes

'Ad ogni costo' is a standard Italian idiom for 'at all costs'. 'Scoprir' has apocope before the ellipsis.
Vien mastro Ford! Salvatevi!: Master Ford is coming! Save yourselves!
The comic farce suddenly turns dangerous: Quickly bursts back in with genuine alarm because Ford really IS coming with an armed mob!
È come una tempesta!: Quickly describes Ford's tempestuous approach using storm imagery ('come una tempesta').
Strepita, tuona, fulmina,: He rants, thunders, strikes like lightning,

Strepita, tuona, fulmina,.meaning: he roars / makes a racket (3rd sing. present)
he strikes like lightning / fulminates (3rd sing. present)

Strepita, tuona, fulmina,: A dramatic tricolon of meteorological verbs conveying Ford's furious tempest of jealousy ('strepita, tuona, fulmina').
si dà dei pugni in testa,: he punches himself in the head,
Comically vivid description of Ford beating his own head with his fists in an uncontrollable fit of fury.
'Scoppiare in' means to burst forth into. 'Urla' is the collective feminine plural of 'urlo'.
Dassenno oppur da burla?: In earnest or as a joke?

Dassenno oppur da burla?.meaning: or / or else (apocopic form of oppure)

Dassenno oppur da burla?: Alice asks Quickly whether Ford's arrival is real ('dassenno') or part of their joke ('da burla').
Dassenno. Egli scavalca: In earnest. He is leaping over

Dassenno. Egli scavalca.meaning: climbs over / scales / vaults (3rd sing. present)

Dassenno. Egli scavalca: Quickly confirms that this is deadly serious: Ford is literally vaulting over walls in his frenzy.
Ford has abandoned the paths and is charging straight through the garden hedges ('le siepi del giardino').
lo segue una gran calca: Inversion: direct object 'lo' precedes verb 'segue' and subject 'una gran calca' (a great mob of followers).
of people... he is already near...
Quickly conveys the rapid approach of the armed mob with fragmented, urgent phrasing.
Mentr'io vi parlo ei valca: While I speak to you he crosses

Mentr'io vi parlo ei valca.meaning: crosses / steps over (3rd sing. present, poetic for varcare)

Mentr'io vi parlo ei valca: 'Valcare' is an archaic/poetic Tuscan variant of 'varcare' (to step over a threshold), rhyming with 'scavalca' and 'calca'.
Quickly is cut off as Ford's shout suddenly echoes right from the doorway.
Malandrino!: Ford's thunderous entrance shout: 'Malandrino!' (scoundrel/brigand), hunting for the seducer he believes is inside.
Il diavolo cavalca: Falstaff groans from behind the screen: this begins Boito's direct translation of Shakespeare's proverb from Henry IV Part 1.
sull'arco di un violino!: upon the bow of a violin!
Falstaff completes Shakespeare's famous quip: 'The devil rides upon a fiddlestick!' (Henry IV Part 1), meaning utter chaos has erupted.
Alice, Meg, Quickly, mr. Ford, poi subit: Alice, Meg, Quickly, Mr. Ford, then immediately Dr. Caius, then Fenton, then
Stage direction describing the cascading mass entrance into the room as Ford's search party floods in.
Bardolfo e Pistola, poi Nannetta. Falsta: Bardolfo and Pistola, then Nannetta. Falstaff still hidden behind the screen.
Stage direction establishing the ensemble layout: all principal characters fill the room while Falstaff quakes in terror behind the screen.
Chiudete le porte! Sbarrate le scale!: Shut the doors! Bar the stairways!
Ford barks urgent military commands with imperative verbs ('Chiudete', 'Sbarrate') to seal every exit.
Seguitemi a caccia! Scoviamo il cignale!: Follow me to the hunt! Let us flush out the boar!

Seguitemi a caccia! Scoviamo il cignale!.meaning: let us flush out / unearth (1st plural imperative)

Seguitemi a caccia! Scoviamo il cignale!: Ford compares hunting Falstaff to flushing out a wild boar ('cignale', archaic Tuscan for cinghiale) from the brush.
Run on the tracks, on the scent.
'Usta' is a specialized Italian hunting term denoting the warm, lingering body scent left behind by wild game.
Tu fruga: Ford barks an urgent imperative command to a follower to rummage every corner of the house.
'Anditi' refers to narrow domestic hallways or corridors connecting rooms.
A caccia!: Bardolfo and Pistola eagerly echo Ford's rallying cry ('A caccia!'), joining the hunt against their former master.
Sventate la fuga!: Ford shouts to cut off any retreat ('sventare la fuga' = to foil or prevent the escape).
Cercate là dentro!: Ford gestures toward an adjacent room, ordering his posse inside as the frantic search continues.
